title: Home to Lagos and a 25-Month Wait: How Tayo Oviosu Started Paga
dek: After thirteen years in the United States, Tayo Oviosu moved back to Lagos in 2008, chose the problem of cash from a list of twenty ideas, and waited more than two years for a licence.

story.event: Returning from Silicon Valley to Lagos and founding a mobile payments company to replace cash
story.summary: Tayo Oviosu left a corporate development job at Cisco in San Jose and returned to Lagos in 2008 to work in private equity, then in April 2009 founded Paga with Jay Alabraba to let Nigerians pay and send money by phone instead of cash. He self-funded the first months; by his account the Central Bank of Nigeria licence took 25 months and the Series A another seven, with a first service running in 2011 and a commercial launch in August 2012. By 2019 Paga reported more than 12 million customers and 20,000 agents.
paragraphs: In 2008, after about thirteen years in the United States, Tayo Oviosu moved back to Lagos. He had studied electrical engineering at the University of Southern California, taken an MBA at Stanford and worked in corporate development at Cisco in San Jose, where he helped lead the company's investments in Africa. When he graduated in 2005, business contacts in Nigeria had told him not to come back; the country, he said, was still about who you knew. He went anyway, to a vice-president's job at Travant Capital Partners, a private equity firm investing in West Africa.

He stayed about five months. While at the firm he drew up a list of about twenty business ideas, and one stood out: cash. Nigerians had plenty of mobile phones but little access to financial services, about four in five residents, by a 2012 estimate, had no formal bank account, and most merchants would not take debit cards, so paying anyone meant carrying money. Oviosu believed, he told Stanford's business school, that "mobile is to Africa as computing was to the Western World." Friends warned him he was heading into uncharted waters.

In April 2009 he started Paga with a fellow Stanford graduate, Jay Alabraba. He paid for the first six months from his savings, and early backers included his former boss, friends and relatives. The longer wait was for permission. By his count it took 25 months to get Paga's licence from the Central Bank of Nigeria and another seven to close its first major funding round. A first service was running in 2011 through small shops acting as agents, where customers paid in cash to fund accounts on their phones, and by the year's end it had about 42,000 customers. Oviosu dates the commercial launch to August 2012.

The question he kept in front of the team, he later said, was "how do I get the market woman in Ajegunle to use this." By 2019 the four people who started Paga had become more than 460, and it reported over 12 million customers, more than 20,000 agents, mostly in rural and semi-rural areas, and $34.7 million raised.

quote.text: The home is the abiding place; in the home is reality; the home helps to attain Him Who is real. So stay where you are, and all things shall come to you in time.
quote.locator: Song XL (I. 65, "avadhû bhûle ko ghar lâwe")
quote.source_title: Songs of Kabir, tr. Rabindranath Tagore, Project Gutenberg eBook #6519
quote.connection: Kabir, defending ordinary household life against those who leave for the forest, finds what is real at home and promises that things come in time. Oviosu spent thirteen years away before coming home, then waited more than two years for a licence. Kabir's patience sounds simple; living it took savings and stubbornness.

reflection: Oviosu's advantage was not a new invention. He knew, from daily life, how awkward it was to carry cash in Nigeria, and he chose to build where that problem lived. Then he waited more than two years for permission to begin properly.

You also work close to problems you know from the inside, and some of what you want to do will wait on someone else's approval. Kabir's advice to stay where you are is not the same as doing nothing. It can mean keeping the work steady, and your own life in order, while the slow part takes its time.
invitation: Name one thing you are waiting on that someone else must approve. Write down one piece of the work around it that needs nobody's permission, and do only that today.

cross_checks.claim: Oviosu returned to Nigeria in 2008 after about thirteen years in the United States
Before Paga he worked at Cisco in San Jose and then at Travant Capital Partners in West Africa
Paga was founded in Lagos in 2009
Paga needed Central Bank of Nigeria approval before it could operate
Paga was started to tackle Nigerians' reliance on cash, with phones as the channel

research_notes: The slate described the episode as leaving Silicon Valley to build mobile payments; the sources show he left Cisco for a private equity job in Lagos in 2008 (five months at Travant, per We Are Tech Africa) and founded Paga in April 2009, so the story tells it in that order. Launch date conflict: Stanford GSB (January 2012) says Paga officially opened in early 2011 and had more than 42,000 customers by the end of that year; Oviosu, quoted by BusinessDay (2019), says it took 25 months to get the licence and seven more to close the Series A, and that Paga took its services to market in August 2012; a Wikipedia mirror says Paga received a full mobile money licence in August 2011. The story gives both, attributing the 25 months and the August 2012 date to Oviosu and the 2011 service to Stanford GSB. The six months of self-funding and the former boss, friends and relatives as early investors rest on Nairametrics' profile alone and are not treated as pivotal. Outcome numbers vary by date: 42,000 customers (end of 2011), 8.2 million users and 15,000 agents (2018, Nairametrics), more than 12 million customers and 20,000 agents (2019, BusinessDay), 19 million registered users and 27,000 agents (2023, We Are Tech Africa); the story uses only the dated 2011 and 2019 figures. The four-in-five unbanked figure is the one Stanford GSB reported in 2012. The Ajegunle remark is from 2021 as quoted by We Are Tech Africa. TechCabal, The Guardian (Nigeria), Techpoint and Paga's own Medium history could not be read and are not cited. Kabir's song defends household life against renunciation in the forest; it is applied by analogy.
